ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Baseline Deterministic Nowcasting Models
PROPOSAL: Compare several state-of-the-art deep learning models for deterministic precipitation nowcasting on a variety of weather radar datasets, including the USE2 radar dataset commonly used in the field, and evaluate their performance on metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). The models to be evaluated are ConvLSTM, PredRNN, Earthformer, and Earthfarseer.
CONTROLS: Implement each model from scratch and use their default configurations (no fine-tuning allowed).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect Earthformer and Earthfarseer to perform significantly better than the other two models. High MAE values are expected due to the time-critical nature of nowcasting and the difficulty of capturing complex precipitation patterns. Potential failure: predicted performance might not be representative of future implementations or model variants.

This experiment aims to establish a strong baseline for future experiments evaluating probabilistic nowcasting models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Probabilistic Nowcasting using Quantile Regression Flow
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel probabilistic nowcasting approach based on Quantile Regression Flows (QRFs), which are differentiable and impose no requirement for neural network training. The QRF will be designed to model the cumulative distribution function of precipitation, allowing for efficient computation of quantile forecasts at multiple lead times. Since the QRF learns a probabilistic distribution directly, it will capture complex and non-linear patterns in the atmospheric data. Evaluation will be performed on various metrics, including MAE, CRPS, and the Hit Rate for events.
CONTROLS: Compare QRF against the deterministic models used in proposal 1, and also consider a diffusion-based model as an additional baseline.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected significant improvement in CRPS and MAE scores compared to the baseline models, demonstrating the capability of QRFs for efficient and effective probabilistic nowcasting. Potential failure: additional runtime complexity associated with inference of the QRF might offset the potential gains in efficiency. 

This proposal aims to reduce the reliance on expensive iterative denoising processes in diffusion models while still generating sharp and reliable ensemble forecasts.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Probabilistic Nowcasting using Quantile Regression Flow
PROPOSAL: Introduce a neural architecture enhancement to the existing Quantile Regression Flow (QRF) model in proposal 2, allowing for time-dependent conditional quantiles. This enables the model to capture time-varying relationships in the cumulative distribution function and turbulent precipitation patterns that emerge over the forecast horizon. We will investigate the use of a CNN structure to extract spatial dependencies in radar data, combined with an LSTM block to incorporate temporal context into the QRF architecture. The enhanced QRF will be evaluated against its base version and diffusion-based baselines, with a particular focus on extreme precipitation events.
CONTROLS: Evaluate both the quality (MAE, CRPS) and diversity of forecast ensembles under the new and base QRF architectures.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvements in Hit Rate for extreme precipitation events, and increases in forecast quality metrics such as CRPS. This will highlight the benefits of incorporating time dependencies in probabilistic nowcasting models, particularly in environments sensitive to loss of possible high-impact events.

This modification will give insight into whether regional, seasonal or temporal variations cause predictability differences.

TITLE: Simplified and Efficient Diffusion Model for Precipitation Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a simplified version of the diffusion model, known as the Forward Diffusion Model (FDM), which reduces the number of iterative denoising steps by half, resulting in significant reductions in computational overhead and memory requirements. This is achieved by exploiting the structure of the radar data and its evolution over time. The model will be trained and evaluated on precipitation nowcasting tasks using metrics such as CRPS, MAE, and the Hit Rate for extreme precipitation events. The performance of the FDM will be compared to the full diffusion model and other baselines to determine its effectiveness as a practical nowcasting tool.
CONTROLS: Compare the FDM against both the base diffusion model and the enhanced QRF model from proposal 2, as well as the deterministic nowcasting models used in proposal 1.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected significant reduction in computational time without sacrificing too much forecast quality, especially at shorter lead times where radar data evolves smoothly. However, performance may degrade at longer lead times due to the reduced depth of the denoising process.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Simplified and Efficient Diffusion Model for Precipitation Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: In addition to the simplified diffusion model proposed in proposal 3, further optimize its hyperparameters through a grid search within a small fraction of the original search space, focusing on those related to the number of iterations, temperature scheduling, and step-size. We will also evaluate the importance of input conditioning, specifically exploring the impact of applying normalization, scaling, or both to the input data before inputting it into the model.
CONTROLS: Compare performance metrics (CRPS, MAE, Hit Rate) of the optimized FDM against its original version, as well as the full diffusion model, the enhanced QRF model, and the deterministic nowcasting models used in proposal 1.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in forecast quality, likely driven by optimizing of the hyperparameters. However, it might not be possible to achieve the level of performance as the full diffusion model, especially at higher lead times where the benefits of the simplified approach are likely to diminish.

TITLE: Ensemble Methods for Improving Probabilistic Nowcasting with Limited Function Evaluations
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of ensemble methods to combine forecasts from the simplified diffusion model, the enhanced Quantile Regression Flow model, and the deterministic nowcasting models used in proposal 1. Specifically, investigate the use of a neural network-based model to learn an optimal combination of the individual forecasts, aiming to leverage their strengths and mitigate their weaknesses. The ensemble method will be evaluated using metrics such as CRPS, MAE, and the Hit Rate for extreme precipitation events, and its performance will be compared to that of the individual models.
CONTROLS: Compare the ensemble method against each of the individual models, as well as the FDM employed in proposal 3 and the enhanced QRF model from proposal 2.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in forecast quality, driven by the ensemble method's ability to combine the strengths of multiple models. However, the success of the ensemble approach relies heavily on the properties of the individual models and might not always lead to better performance.

TITLE: Investigating Conditional Normalizing Flows for Precipitation Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: We train a conditional normalizing flow (CNF) model on the ChoLPI dataset (resolution: 2 km, mesh size: 250 m, time step: 15 minutes) and evaluate its performance against a variety of baselines, including a deterministic transformer-based model (Earthformer).
CONTROLS: 
- Baselines: Earthformer, Eulerian persistence, Lagrangian persistence.
- Variation of conditional independence structure, the number of flows, and the number of layers.
COST: 4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This CNF model is expected to improve upon the predictive power of deterministic models, especially for shorter lead times (up to 1 hour), but may struggle to capture extreme precipitation events. It is unclear whether the detailed spatial structures of clouds and precipitation can be effectively represented through a flow, and embeddings of the current precipitation field might not be learned accurately due to the input curse.

The experimental design in this proposal is kept relatively simple to gauge the efficiency and performance of CNFs for precipitation nowcasting. The choice of ChoLPI and Earthformer models as baselines ensures a reasonable starting point for evaluating the nowcasting abilities of CNFs.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hybrid Non-linear Temporal Fusion (HNTF) for Efficient Precipitation Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid non-linear temporal fusion (HNTF) framework to efficiently generate ensemble forecasts. HNTF combines the strengths of diffusion models (latent diffusion models) and timestep-based fusion, which incorporates physical intuition about atmospheric processes to effectively model temporal dependencies.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare HNTF with the baseline diffusion model and the deterministic Earthformer model.
- Vary the capacity of the diffusion model and the strength of the physical prior.
- Include experiments using two different precipitation datasets: ChoLPI and the more challenging operational radar imaging dataset, DKRZ-ERAD.
COST: 6 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should demonstrate decreased computational cost while maintaining good performance, and such a trade-off is necessary for time-critical precipitation nowcasting. If well-designed, HNTF can achieve state-of-the-art performance with lower computational costs than diffusion models.

By combining the strengths of two different techniques, this method offers an efficient framework capable of modeling non-linear temporal dependencies, which is beneficial in high-dimensional spatiotemporal nowcasting.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Assessing the Effectiveness of Multi-Scale Fusion for Precipitation Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the benefits of multi-scale fusion in precipitation nowcasting by combining the strengths of Earthformer and a downscaled conditioned diffusion model. This strategy aims to capture global atmospheric patterns while providing detailed prediction of precipitation fields at higher resolutions.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the multi-scale fusion model with individual Earthformer and the diffusion model.
- Vary the downsampling ratio and the complexity of the diffusion model.
- Include the more challenging dataset, DKRZ-ERAD, and evaluate predictions for extreme weather events.
COST: 8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is predicted to effectively improve the nowcasting performance by combining strong global atmospheric predictions and additional local-scale precipitation details. The effectiveness of multi-scale fusion, however, heavily relies on the accurate downsampling ratio and the complexity of the diffusion model.

By assessing the effectiveness of this multi-scale fusion strategy, this proposal aims to quantify the benefits of combining different models and exploring the optimal fusion architecture for precipitation nowcasting.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Improving the Assessing the Effectiveness of Multi-Scale Fusion for Precipitation Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hierarchical fusion strategy, combining a high-resolution Earthformer with a prediction refinement mechanism via a low-dimensional conditional diffusion model. This refinement mechanism takes the high-resolution output from the Earthformer and refines the details of the precipitation field, particularly focusing on extreme events and those with complex spatial structures.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the proposed hierarchical fusion with a simple concatenative fusion strategy.
- Vary the complexity of the low-dimensional diffusion model and the choice of temperature parameter.
- Include experiments using real-world weather radar images, specifically for predicting high-impact weather events.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hierarchical fusion approach should improve nowcasting performance by accurately refining high-resolution precipitation fields, especially for extreme events. The success of the hierarchical fusion, however, depends on designing an effective refinement mechanism and selecting an appropriate low-dimensional diffusion model.

The revised proposal focuses on the intricacies of precipitation nowcasting, specifically the refinement mechanism and its potential to capture extreme events and complex spatial structures.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Stochastic Weather Radar Image Discourse
PROPOSAL: We introduce a transformer-based stochastic weather radar image discourse (SWIRD) model to generate diverse precipitation forecasts by incorporating uncertainty from multiple sensor measurements. SWIRD utilizes attentional mechanisms to weigh different radar sources and learn a compact representation of uncertainty in precipitation fields.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare SWIRD with the deterministic Earthformer and the HNTF model.
- Vary the number of radar sources and the attention mechanism.
- Include experiments using both ChoLPI and DKRZ-ERAD datasets.
COST: 8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This stochastic model is expected to capture uncertainty in precipitation forecasts and generate a set of diverse and plausible futures. Its performance may be compromised by its tendency to overestimate uncertainty, and it's uncertain whether its attentional mechanisms can effectively handle large numbers of radar sources.

The SWIRD model allows the incorporation of uncertainty from multiple sensor measurements, providing a novel approach to precipitation nowcasting that captures the inherent complexity and unpredictability of weather systems.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Investigating Transfer Learning for Precipitation Nowcasting Across Different Radar Systems
PROPOSAL: We explore the application of transfer learning for nowcasting across different radar systems, aiming to develop a single model that can effectively adapt to various radar types, resolutions, and operational settings. This is achieved by fine-tuning a pre-trained Earthformer model on specific radar datasets and evaluating its performance across different scenarios.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the fine-tuned Earthformer with a model trained from scratch for each radar system.
- Vary the choice of pre-training dataset, fine-tuning strategy, and number of adaptation layers.
- Include experiments using both ChoLPI and DKRZ-ERAD datasets, as well as real-world radar systems.
COST: 12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This transfer learning approach is expected to improve adaptability and reduce the need for domain-specific training data, allowing for widespread adoption of precipitation nowcasting models across different radar systems. However, it may struggle to capture nuances specific to individual radar systems, and the choice of pre-training dataset and fine-tuning strategy will be critical.

The investigation of transfer learning aims to leverage the widespread deployment of radar systems, reducing the need for extensive fine-tuning and enabling more efficient precipitation nowcasting across varying scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Probabilistic Sampling-Based Storm Surge Nowcasting
PROPOSAL: We introduce a probabilistic sampling-based storm surge nowcasting framework that incorporates the uncertainties associated with storm track and intensity forecasts. This framework utilizes a conditional normalizing flow to model the distribution of possible storm paths and latent physical parameters, enabling the generation of multi-future storm surge predictions for improved decision-making.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the proposed framework with traditional deterministic storm surge models.
- Vary the complexity of the conditional normalizing flow and the sampling strategy.
- Include experiments with high-resolution, storm-resolving radar data (e.g., DKRZ-ERAD) and evaluate predictions for extreme storm events.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This framework should improve nowcasting performance by quantifying and propagating uncertainties in storm forecasts, ultimately allowing for more accurate and reliable storm surge predictions. However, accurately modeling the distribution of possible storm paths and latent physical parameters may be challenging, and the sampling strategy may require careful tuning.

The new framework aims to address the challenges associated with predicting storm surges by leveraging probabilistic modeling and sampling techniques, enabling the generation of multiple future scenarios for critical decision-making applications.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Spatial and Temporal Context on Precipitation Nowcasting Models
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the impact of incorporating spatial and temporal context into precipitation nowcasting models, specifically exploring the benefits of using spatial context (e.g., neighboring radar beams) and temporal context (e.g., past weather patterns) in combination with traditional physic-based models.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare performances with and without the incorporation of spatial and temporal context.
- Vary the radius of spatial context and time window for temporal context.
- Include experiments using ChoLPI and DKRZ-ERAD datasets and evaluate predictions for varying precipitation intensity and event types.
COST: 8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study will provide insights into the benefits and limitations of incorporating spatial and temporal context into precipitation nowcasting models, potentially leading to improved predictive performance and a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physical processes.

The new proposal aims to investigate the practical applications of incorporating spatial and temporal context, which can help capture the complex relationships between precipitation events and their surrounding environment. By assessing the impact of these factors, the study can contribute to the development of more accurate and robust meteorological models.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Conditional Normalizing Flows for Precipitation Nowcasting with Spatially-Variant Noise Injection
PROPOSAL: We modify the conditional normalizing flow (CNF) architecture to incorporate spatially-variant noise injection, allowing the model to adapt to the varying structures and complexities of precipitation fields across different spatial regions. This adaptation enables more accurate prediction of precipitation fields with diverse spatial characteristics.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare CNF with spatially-variant noise injection to the original CNF architecture.
- Vary the noise injection strategy and the spatial support size.
- Include experiments using ChoLPI and DKRZ-ERAD datasets and evaluate predictions for varying precipitation intensity and event types.
COST: 6 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised CNF model with spatially-variant noise injection should demonstrate improved performance by capturing the unique spatial characteristics of precipitation fields and adapting to the diverse spatial structures present in the data, particularly in the case of complex precipitation events.

The revised CNF model builds upon the original proposal by introducing a critical component that better captures the spatial complexities of precipitation fields, likely leading to improved predictive performance.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Benchmarking and Ensembling Precipitation Nowcasting Models for Operational Weather Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We establish a comprehensive benchmark platform to evaluate and compare the performance of the proposed and existing precipitation nowcasting models, including deterministic and probabilistic architectures. Furthermore, we explore ensemble techniques to combine predictions from multiple models, aiming to develop a robust operational weather forecasting system.
CONTROLS: 
- Evaluate and compare multiple nowcasting models using a range of metrics and evaluation datasets.
- Vary ensemble techniques and model combinations to identify the most effective ensemble setup.
- Include real-world experiments and evaluate predictions for critical weather events and operational scenarios.
COST: 15 GPU-hours ( combinatorial/exhaustive with varying combinations of complexity)
PREDICTION: This benchmarking and ensemble framework is expected to provide a solid foundation for operational weather forecasting by identifying the strengths and weaknesses of individual models, and ultimately developing a robust ensemble system capable of accurately predicting precipitation events in various scenarios.

The addition of this final proposal completes the set of experiments and theoretical results, providing a comprehensive approach to precipitation nowcasting. The benchmarking and ensemble framework offers a versatile platform for future research and development, allowing for exploration of novel architectures and ensemble techniques in the context of real-world operational scenarios.
